chapters.relation: Dan Geva re-reads Dziga Vertov's The Man with the Movie Camera as a coherent philosophy of documentary he calls 'praxis' or 'cine-seeing the invisible,' distilling ten 'diktats' (Unplayed Cinema, Life-Caught-Unawares, the interval theory of montage, etc.). He argues Vertov, like Plato, Marx, Nietzsche and Freud, privileges hidden depths over surface appearance, and reads the dialectical move from 'film fact' to 'film thing' as a Hegelian synthesis rather than a paradox. Crucially he aligns Vertov's Kino-Eye truth with Heidegger's notion of truth as aletheia (a partial unconcealment) rather than correspondence, tying the camera's revelation of the invisible to Heidegger's meditation on technology and seeing.

Elan Gamaker analyzes Ken Loach's Cathy Come Home and Ken Russell's London Moods and Shelagh Delaney's Salford as British social-realist 'documentary style,' arguing that agency (in the Marxist sense of free choice against structure) is progressively eroded from funder to filmmaker to subject to viewer. He shows how Grierson's neo-Hegelian faith in state institutions turned documentary into 'good propaganda' that alienates the underclass it claims to serve, so the form reproduces cultural hegemony and false consciousness. Loach's stylization and Russell's ambiguity strip the depicted subjects of voice, though Gamaker holds that a later viewer's shifting interpretation can partly restore agency.

Selmin Kara reads Victor Erice's Dream of Light (The Quince Tree Sun), about the painter Antonio Lopez trying to capture a quince tree in shifting autumn light, as a case for a 'new materialist' ontology of documentary against Bill Nichols-style representationalism. Drawing on Deleuze via De Landa's actual/virtual continuum, Spinoza's and Bergson's vital-matter lineage, and Bennett's 'vibrant matter,' she argues the film's dream sequence of the operator-less camera, dimmer and rotting fruit foregrounds the mediation rather than the mastery of light. She proposes updating Grierson's 'creative treatment of actuality' to 'the creative treatment of actuality and virtuality,' treating filmic and profilmic matter as intra-acting agents.

Rick Altman dismantles four and a half 'fallacies' that let film theory ignore sound: the historical fallacy (sound as a late add-on), the ontological fallacy (image alone is cinema), the reproductive fallacy (recording reproduces rather than represents sound), the nominalist fallacy, and the half-fallacy of indexicality. In the nominalist section he explicitly frames the dispute over whether the 'same' sound heard from different seats shares a real identity as the medieval realism-versus-nominalism debate, casting Plato and Augustine as the realists and William of Ockham as the nominalist, and warning that ultra-nominalism about sound jeopardizes shared understanding. He uses Peirce's index/icon/symbol distinction to argue electronics has desacralized cinema's indexicality.

Lars von Trier and Thomas Vinterberg's DOGMA 95 manifesto and its 'Vow of Chastity' declare a rescue action against the 'individual film,' the auteur concept (dismissed as bourgeois romanticism) and the cinema of illusion and cosmetic trickery. The ten vows bind the director to location shooting, diegetic sound, handheld camera, no optical work, no superficial action or genre, the here-and-now, and no directorial credit, swearing off personal taste in order to 'force the truth out of' characters and settings. As a primary-source polemic it advances an anti-illusionist, anti-individualist ethic of documentary-adjacent truth-telling rather than applying any named philosopher.

Werner Herzog's Minnesota Declaration is a thirteen-point primary-source polemic attacking Cinema Verite as 'the truth of accountants' that confounds fact with truth and merely photographs the 'ancient ruins of facts.' Herzog insists on a deeper 'poetic, ecstatic truth' that is mysterious and reachable only through fabrication, imagination and stylization, illustrated by his own Lessons of Darkness. The aphorisms about indifferent nature, the merciless ocean and 'you can't legislate stupidity' assert that documentary illumination lies beyond mere factual accuracy, but the piece names no philosopher and applies no taxonomy concept directly.

V. F. Perkins performs a close reading of the final four-minute shot of Frederick Wiseman's High School, where principal Dr. Haller reads a soldier's letter from Vietnam ('I am only a body doing a job') and claims it proves the school's success. Against the critical consensus (Kael, Bordwell and Thompson) that fixes only on the 'body doing a job' line, Perkins recovers two overlooked features: the gendered, maternal significance of the female reader, and Wiseman's stealthy editorial dropping of the sound a half-second before the image fades, leaving the principal's triumphant smile 'hollowed out.' He argues film grades its effects so that meaning can register below conscious notice, and warns that pause-and-rewind analysis steals the filmmaker's control over time, so close reading must stay answerable to a true experience of the movie.

Jennifer McMahon reads Gabriela Cowperthwaite's Blackfish through Thomas Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' and the problem of other minds, arguing the film's interviews with orca neuroscientists (Marino et al.) function as Nagel's proposed 'objective phenomenology,' conveying orca consciousness through objective indicators rather than mere anthropomorphic projection. She dissects the film's rhetoric around Tilikum and Dawn Brancheau, showing how the title, delayed naming, SeaWorld ad juxtapositions and emotional testimony first vilify then humanize the whale to argue captivity is morally unacceptable. Invoking Peggy Zeglin Brand's 'lenses,' Iris Murdoch's 'unselfing' and Marc Bekoff's inclusive ethic, she concludes the film approximates truth about orca minds even as it, like SeaWorld, is 'structured to sell.'

Keith Dromm argues against the 'assertoric view' of documentary (Carroll's presumptive assertion, Currie's photographic traces, Plantinga's asserted veridical representation), contending that documentary films aim less to make assertions than to promote understanding. Drawing on Elgin, Zagzebski and Kvanvig on understanding as a holistic, skill-like cognitive success, and on Wittgenstein's Philosophical Investigations account of how understanding is taught through examples, practice and 'perspicuous representation,' he shows how Resnais's Night and Fog, Ken Burns, Errol Morris and Frederick Wiseman convey an understanding of their subject through creative technique. He treats reenactments as scientific-model-like idealizations that serve understanding even when they depart from literal truth.

K. L. Evans argues that Adam McKay's The Big Short is fiction that nonetheless borrows documentary's assertive stance to make true claims about the 2008 subprime crisis and to insist ordinary viewers are smart enough to 'read the signs.' Using Aristotle on fiction (concerned with meaning not fact), Auerbach and the Heraclitean maxim that 'a man's character is his fate,' she distinguishes real people from 'characters' (living images) like the film's Michael Burry and Billy Beane, arguing that casting Brad Pitt signals the fictive stance. She invokes Deleuze's question about the 'mode of existence' of whoever pronounces a proposition to explain how the unreliable narrator Vennett can still narrate reliably, and how the film embeds indigestible factual 'markers' to refute the idea that the crisis was too complex to understand.

Bill Nichols writes an open letter to Errol Morris explaining his bodily 'revulsion' at Standard Operating Procedure, Morris's film on the Abu Ghraib torture photographs. Nichols gives three reasons: the painfully limited, remorseless perspective of the MP guards elevated to mythic screen scale; the morally impossible reenactment tracking shots that put the viewer in the torturers' point of view (compared to Schindler's List); and the total absence of the Iraqi detainees' voices. He faults Morris for decontextualizing and fetishizing the images and forfeiting a moral center, contrasting the film with Rithy Panh's S-21, and casts the missing ethical encounter in terms of Buber's I-Thou relation of mutual honesty while wishing he had Fanon's capacity to treat the perpetrators' suffering.

Michael Fried reads Douglas Gordon and Philippe Parreno's Zidane: A Twenty-First Century Portrait, seventeen synchronized cameras trained on Zinedine Zidane through one Real Madrid match, as a portrait that lays bare a new relation between absorption and being-beheld. Set within Fried's own absorption/theatricality tradition, the film shows Zidane wholly absorbed yet acutely conscious of eighty thousand spectators ('you are never alone'), which Fried reads via Heidegger's notion that even this 'bare' absorbed consciousness discloses a shared world (underscored by the halftime global news montage). He then stages the film as evidence in the McDowell-Dreyfus dispute over whether perception is conceptual, arguing that Zidane's 'expert coping' looks 'permeated by mindedness' (McDowell) rather than the non-conceptual absorbed coping Dreyfus, following Merleau-Ponty's embodied phenomenology, describes.
